newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-PENALTY RULE CHANGE COULD END PLAYERS' HEARTBREAK.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-PENALTY RULE CHANGE COULD END PLAYERS' HEARTBREAK.

text.p: The sight of heartbroken footballers collapsing in tears after missing the decisive penalty in a shoot-out is likely to become a thing of the past following a recommendation by FIFA's influential referees' committee on Tuesday.

The committee approved a proposal, which is virtually certain to be rubber-stamped by the executive committee, that the penalty shootout can now be held in a drawn match at the end of 90 minutes and before the start of extra time.
Extra time will still be played, with the winners of the shootout winning the match if extra time also ends in a draw.
By having the penalties before extra time, the player who missed the decisive penalty would have a chance to redeem himself in the extra period and his team a second chance to win the match.

The recommendation comes under FIFA's regulations rather than under the Laws of the Game and as such does not need the approval of the International Board, which meets annually to consider law changes. Its next meeting is in Belfast on March 1.

FIFA spokesman Andreas Herren said: "The decision means that from next season, and pending the final approval of the executive committee, if a national association wants to organise its cup competition using this method they are free to do so. Likewise UEFA, for example, could introduce this at the next European championship and FIFA at the World Cup finals."

The most recent examples of heartbreak for players came in last year's European championship in England with both England and France losing their semifinals on penalties. Spain and the Netherlands were also eliminated on penalties in the quarter-finals.
David Davies, the English F.A.'s director of communications, said the proposal should be given some very serious consideration.
"As people will know there have been several proposals in recent times aimed particularly at making the penalty shootout less traumatic, especially for players.
"We would anticipate some lively debate in England before this proposal would be introduced in any of our domestic competitions."

The referees' committee meeting, chaired by David Will, considered a number of points, all designed to make the game Some of the points regarding the laws of the game can be introduced only after being approved by the International Board. Included in these is the proposal that in future goalkeepers will be allowed to move along their line at a penalty kick.
The meeting also backed the proposal to ban a goalkeeper from holding the ball unneccesarily for longer than five seconds and called for a stricter application of the four-step rule.
As expected, the committee will propose to the International Board that the backpass rule should be extended to all parts of the body which would outlaw headers and throw-ins back to the goalkeeper.

The committee re-iterated the ruling taken before the 1994 World Cup finals that tackles from behind should be punished by a red card and also called for players who "scored" a goal by a deliberate handball to be sent off.

But it strongly opposed the idea of having two referees controlling the match and also strongly rejected experiments with electronic line-judges and field-side TV monitors to decide controversial situations.

The committee also came out strongly against anyone other than the referee keeping time, but agreed to wait for the result of an experiment ntly underway in Italy by which the referee tells the fourth official how many minutes he intends to play over 45 minutes, with the fourth official informing the spectators.
In another move aimed at encroaching technology in the sport, the committee condemmed the use of action replays on giant screens at all FIFA matches.
"We want to retain the authority of the referee as much as possible" said Herren, "and we feel that these measures will help us do that."

Two ideas sidelined for the time being were for an automatic sending-off after a certain number of fouls, as that point is already covered in the Laws with punishment for "persistent infringement", and introducing kick-ins -- last a feature of the game in the 1870s -- to replace throw-ins.
The committee discussed the golden goal rule but made no recommendation about its future.
